paras: The Hamburg shooting and threatened lynching of Harry Hackett took place on the afternoon of Thursday, January 13, 1881, in Hamburg, South Carolina, when Hackett, a Black man, fired at a white man named Damm after a quarrel and the bullet struck and mortally wounded Damm's wife.
Hackett escaped, reportedly across the river to Augusta, Georgia, and South Carolina papers reported that a party was hunting him and that he would be lynched if caught.
No report of his capture or fate appears in the coverage.
According to the Augusta Chronicle, Hackett was employed by a Mr. Roll, the brother-in-law of George W. Damm, known as Willie Damm, whose residence adjoined Roll's store.
Damm was preparing to go to Augusta with his wife to visit relatives on her birthday, and she had been married about a year.
At about four o'clock Hackett walked up and stood listening while Damm talked with his wife and sister, and Damm told him he had no business there and ordered him away.
In the Chronicle's version Damm, when Hackett was slow to leave, "kicked at him"; the News and Courier dispatch mentions only the order to leave.
Both versions say Hackett put his hand behind him as if to draw a pistol, and that Damm went after him but was held back by his wife and sister.
Hackett then fired at Damm from behind the counter of Roll's store, missing him and striking Mrs. Damm in the head.
Damm followed Hackett into the street, where Hackett fired three more shots, one of which grazed Damm's right shoulder and another of which burned his face with powder.
The Chronicle added that Damm, who had no weapon, threw a razor hone that struck Hackett on the head and grappled with him before Hackett broke loose and escaped.
A search was organized at once, and the Chronicle reported that "threats were freely made" that if Hackett were caught "the law would not be called upon to punish him."

The News and Courier's correspondent wrote of "much excitement in Hamburg" and predicted that Hackett would be lynched if taken, while the Pickens Sentinel said that "Judge Lynch will doubtless have a case."
The Newberry Herald reported that Hackett had escaped into Georgia.
No report of an arrest, inquest, trial or lynching was found in the coverage.

The surviving coverage comes entirely from the white press of South Carolina and Georgia and rests on two sources: the Augusta Chronicle's on-the-spot report, reprinted by the Savannah Morning News on January 15, and a dispatch from Augusta to the Charleston News and Courier.

The Winnsboro News and Herald ran the dispatch the same day under "A Tragedy in Hamburg," and the Anderson Intelligencer reprinted it on January 20, the day the Pickens Sentinel ran a shorter item headed "Homicide in Hamburg."
The Newberry Herald's brief of January 19 identified Mrs. Damm as "a white woman" and Hackett as "a negro," the only racial labels in most of the items.
The Savannah paper's headline, "Horrible Crime," and the Chronicle's repeated use of "the assassin" presented the Damm family's account as fact, and no paper printed any account from Hackett.
The papers reported the lynching threats as an expected outcome rather than as something to be prevented, and none mentioned officers or a reward.

The papers differ on Mrs. Damm's condition: the Chronicle's reporter found her "in a dying condition" and not expected to live through the night, while the Newberry Herald said the shot killed her instantly and other items called the wound fatal.

They also differ on the setting, the Chronicle placing the first shot in Roll's store next to Damm's residence and the dispatch placing the conversation in Damm's own store, and on Damm's first name, given as George W. or Willie in Augusta and as William in the dispatch.

bases: A white search party pursued Harry Hackett after he shot Mrs. Damm, with threats that he would be lynched if caught (A1, A5, A6); no seizure or killing is reported, so this is a threatened lynching.
The Augusta Chronicle's reporter (A1) and the separate Augusta dispatch to the News and Courier (A2, A6) agree on the shooting, Hackett's escape and the lynch threats; A3 and A5 are short summaries.

accounts.label: Augusta dispatch to the News and Courier
accounts.gist: Damm ordered Hackett away; Hackett reached as if for a pistol and fired, fatally wounding Mrs. Damm; Hackett escaped and would be lynched if caught.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headed the Chronicle's report 'Horrible Crime' and called Hackett 'the assassin', recording the threats to bypass the law without comment.
The News and Herald and the Anderson Intelligencer reprinted the News and Courier dispatch, ending with the prediction that Hackett 'will be lynched'.
The Pickens Sentinel's 'Homicide in Hamburg' closed with 'Judge Lynch will doubtless have a case.'
